title: Zeta resilient GPU pool simulation and cost fallouts
content:
Context:
Customer Zeta is evaluating a Dedicated pool option to host an internal Q&A agent with bursty daily traffic: heavy mornings and lighter afternoons with unpredictable sudden spikes (marketing demo bursts). They need a budget-conscious commitment but also >95% success rate for requests under 500ms P95. This doc captures our resilience-first simulation, fallback scenarios, and a round of cost fallouts for commitment levels and autoscale guards.

Workshop takeaways (raw):
- primary goal: keep tail latency low while limiting committed spend; secondary: graceful quality degradation (model fallback) instead of hard failures.
- traffic profile used: baseline steady 40 qps, morning peak 180 qps for 45 minutes, occasional demo spike up to 400 qps for 5–10 minutes (estimated once per week).
- typical request token distribution: median 120 tokens in, median 80 tokens generated, 98th token length ~800 tokens (rare).
- workload is mixed: short retrieval-style prompts and longer multi-turn summarization. We simulated both mixes.

Simulation model (notes on assumptions):
- GPU types modelled: A100-80GB (on-prem equiv) and H100-floating (cloud equiv).
- per-GPU effective throughput measured as tokens/s under our runtime: A100 = 10k tokens/s mixed precision; H100 = 20k tokens/s when warmed and quantized path used. (These numbers are tool-run inputs; not bench claims.)
- continuous batching: avg batch window 12ms at 60 qps, rising to 30ms at 300 qps in worst case.
- KV-cache hit assumptions: 12% total token save for multi-turn sessions, used in cost sims.
- cold-start penalty: first request to a freshly provisioned GPU has 250ms extra setup (container + model warm).

Design approach (resilience-first):
1) Partition pool into three sub-buckets: committed-reserved, elastic-buffer, and demo-eviction.
   - committed-reserved: capacity equal to expected sustained 99th percentile minus a small headroom. Always-on, covered by commitment discount.
   - elastic-buffer: small set of hot-warm nodes that can be spun up quickly (short-lived on/off). Sized to cover common peaks (10–30% over committed).
   - demo-eviction: low-priority spot-like nodes that can be stolen; used for non-critical/latency-flexible requests (batchable jobs, indexing).
2) Routing policy: latency-first for committed tier, best-effort for elastic, and preemptable for demo-eviction. If elastic unavailable, degrade to model-quantize fallback in committed pool before rejecting.
3) Fallbacks: auto-quantized model (higher perplexity but 2–3x throughput), or model-size fallback (e.g., Llama-70B -> 13B distilled for tail requests). Prefer quantize+cache first.

Autoscale policy (bucket-based):
- metric: observed queue length + P95 latency signal.
- scale-up trigger: sustained queue_length > 0.75 * committed_capacity for 30s or P95 > target_latency for 20s.
- scale-down: sustained queue_length < 0.35 * committed_capacity for 120s and P95 < target_latency for 2m.
- fast-burst protection: for demo spikes, allow short-term bursting to elastic-buffer up to 3x baseline with an enforced cool-down (10m) to avoid oscillation.
- prewarm hedge: keep one warm replica per model-variant in elastic-buffer to service first-request cold penalty.

Sizing scenarios and cost fallouts (monthly cost estimates, rounded)
Assumptions: 720 hours/month, on-demand cloud H100 list price baseline = $30/hr (sim input), committed discount options modeled at 40% for reserved capacity, spot/evictable at 75% discount. A100 on-prem equivalent cost per-hr (amortized) = $8/hr in our scenarios. These numbers are intentionally conservative inputs for customer discussion.

Scenario A (low-commit): commit capacity to cover 60 qps sustained (baseline + small headroom).
- committed GPUs (A100-equivalent): 6 GPUs -> covers ~60 qps steady with buffer. Cost: 6 * $8 * 720 = $34,560/mo.
- elastic buffer: 2 H100 on-demand kept warm half the time (prewarm + occasional spin-ups): 2 * $30 * 360 = $21,600/mo when opportunistically used.
- demo-eviction: no reserved capacity, rely on spot during demos (~8 hours/month total): 2 * $7.5 * 8 = $120/mo.
- effective monthly spend (observed): ~ $56k, with 40% of spend eligible for commitment pricing if moved to H100 reservations.
- risk: frequent demo spikes will push many requests to elastic on-demand increasing variability in cost.

Scenario B (medium-commit, resilience-optimized): commit for 140 qps (covers morning peaks mostly).
- committed GPUs (H100-reserved after discount): 8 H100 reserved (40% discount applied) => effective price $18/hr. Cost: 8 * $18 * 720 = $103,680/mo.
- elastic buffer: 3 H100 on-demand for unexpected 200–400 qps spikes, used averaging 50 hours/month: 3 * $30 * 50 = $4,500/mo.
- demo-eviction: spot nodes handling non-critical batch jobs, ~20 hours/month: 4 * $7.5 * 20 = $600/mo.
- effective monthly spend: ~ $108.8k/mo. Compared to Scenario A: higher committed cash but much lower on-demand variance and better P95 predictability.

Scenario C (high-commit with aggressive fallbacks): commit for full morning peak (200 qps) but enable model-size fallback for tails to reduce GPU count.
- committed: 12 H100-reserved => 12 * $18 * 720 = $155,520/mo.
- elastic buffer: minimal (1 instance warm) => $540/mo (approx).
- fallback savings: by routing 15% of peak traffic to 13B distilled fallback we estimate 30% less GPU-hours during spikes -> net monthly cost down by ~$14k vs naive full-commit.
- effective monthly spend: ~ $142k/mo after fallback savings.
- tradeoffs: quality regression windows when fallback is active; requires monitoring and eval gating.

Tail-risk cost fallouts (what breaks cost model):
- prolonged demo period (e.g., 3 hours straight at 400 qps) consumes elastic buffer and drives many on-demand spins => cost spikes up to +40% for the month unless mitigated by enforced rate-limiter on demo routing or temporary quota.
- model regression flips: if quantized/13B fallback shows unacceptable quality, customer will keep requests on higher-cost variants leading to extra GPU-hours.
- prewarm leaks: if prewarm replicas are kept warm for too many variants, committed cost rises unintentionally.

Operational runbook recommendations (practical):
- Start with Scenario B for POC (provides predictable P95 and shows commitment ROI).
- Configure rollout: enable automatic fallback quantization behind a feature flag with canary traffic (5% -> 20% -> 100%) measured against prompt set.
- Demo policy: separate route for marketing/demo traffic with strict token/time quotas and an enforced cool-down per demo session. Provide a demo-queue admission control so customers see graceful degradation (queued or degraded model) instead of opaque failures.
- Cost alerts: notify when elastic on-demand spend > 25% of committed monthly budget for two consecutive days.

Metrics to collect during POC (minimum):
- per-route token throughput, P95 latency, cold-start counts, prewarm utilization, cache hit rate, fallback activation rate, per-GPU utilization, and hourly spend per GPU category.
- capture a small evaluation prompt set to measure quality delta when fallback engaged.

Open questions and next actions (owners):
- (Maya) run a 2-week stress sim with customer production trace (requested).
- (Arjun) produce a small eval harness to quantify quality vs latency for quantized fallback by 2024-10-03.
- (Lena) prepare an elastic-buffer sizing quick calculator for sales (spreadsheet) and attach to Confluence.
- (Tomás) propose demo-queue admission control mechanics and API changes to the routing layer.

Appendix: quick back-of-envelope P95 latency mapping (sim output):
- Scenario A: P95 ~ 580ms during morning peaks (above target); demo spikes push P95 to 1.1s unless elastic buffer active.
- Scenario B: P95 ~ 420ms typical, 2% tail events hitting fallback with P95 ~ 650ms.
- Scenario C: P95 ~ 380ms baseline, but fidelity drop observed during fallback windows.

Notes to reviewers: this is a working doc — numbers are simulation-derived and meant to guide the customer commitment discussion. We should avoid hard guarantees from these sims until we run a live trace-based POC.
